title: Goecha La and Dzongri trek from Yuksom: a practical guide
summary: The Goecha La trek runs from Yuksom (1,780 m) through Khangchendzonga National Park to viewpoints below the Goecha La pass (4,940 m) facing Kangchenjunga, and usually takes 8–10 days. The shorter Dzongri trek takes 4–5 days. Both need park permits and a registered guide, and are best in April–May and October–November.
meta_description: Goecha La and Dzongri trek guide from Yuksom: day-by-day stages, altitudes, permits, costs, seasons, gear and altitude safety. Indicative 2025–26 prices.

sections.heading: What the trek is and who it suits
paras: The Goecha La trek is the best-known trek in Sikkim. It starts at Yuksom, the village where Sikkim's first king was crowned, and climbs through the forests and high pastures of Khangchendzonga National Park to a series of viewpoints below the Goecha La pass, which stands at about 4,940 m. From there the south-east face of Kangchenjunga, the world's third-highest mountain at 8,586 m, fills the head of the valley.

The full trek usually takes 8–10 days from Yuksom and back. A shorter version turns around at Dzongri, at about 4,000 m, after 4–5 days, and still gives a close dawn view of Kangchenjunga, Kabru, Pandim and the peaks around them from Dzongri Top.

It suits fit walkers with some experience of multi-day hiking. No climbing skill is needed, but days are long, the trail is steep in places and the height gain is fast. Altitude, not fitness alone, is what turns people back. If you have never slept above 3,500 m, build in a rest day and go with a guide who will make you turn around if needed.

sections.heading: Permits, guides and the rules in force
paras: Khangchendzonga National Park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and entry is controlled. Every trekker needs a park entry permit, issued at the forest checkpost in Yuksom, and must register with the police there. Fees are charged per person per day, with higher rates for foreign nationals, plus charges for tents, cameras and pack animals. Amounts change from season to season, so treat any figure you see as indicative.

Independent trekking is not allowed. You must be accompanied by a registered guide, and in practice almost everyone books through a licensed agency in Yuksom or Gangtok, which handles permits, food, tents, porters and pack animals. Foreign nationals also need the Sikkim Inner Line Permit and a trekking permit arranged by a registered Sikkim agency, normally for a group of at least two people.

In recent seasons the authorities have generally allowed trekkers only as far as View Point 1 below the pass, with the final section to the pass itself closed. Rules on how far you can go, on guide numbers and on camping sites have changed several times. Check current status before you travel and ask your agency to confirm the route in writing.
list: Indian trekkers: photo ID, park permit at Yuksom, police registration, registered guide.
Foreign trekkers: passport and visa, Sikkim ILP, trekking permit through a registered agency, group of two or more, registered guide.
Everyone: carry several passport photos and photocopies of ID and permits.

sections.heading: Day by day from Yuksom
paras: The plan below is the most common 8-day itinerary, counting from the first day of walking. Agencies vary it, and many add a second rest day. Altitudes and distances are approximate; take them as a guide to effort rather than exact figures.

Day one is long. The trail leaves the top of Yuksom and follows the Prek Chu valley through warm forest, crossing several suspension bridges to Sachen and then climbing steeply to Bakhim and Tshoka, a small settlement of Tibetan refugees with a lodge and campsites. Day two climbs through rhododendron forest to the clearing at Phedang and on to Dzongri, an open meadow at about 4,000 m. A rest day at Dzongri, with a dawn walk up to Dzongri Top, is strongly advised.

From Dzongri the trail drops to the river at Kokchurang and climbs gently to Thansing, a wide meadow with Pandim towering above. A short day leads to Lamuney, the last campsite. On summit day you start in the dark, pass the glacial Samiti Lake and reach View Point 1 for sunrise on Kangchenjunga, then walk all the way back down to Thansing or Kokchurang. The return to Yuksom takes two more days via Phedang and Tshoka.

sections.heading: When to go
paras: There are two seasons. The spring season, from April to May, brings rhododendrons in full bloom between Tshoka and Phedang, milder nights and longer days, but cloud builds by late morning and views are less reliable. Afternoon showers are common in May.

The autumn season, from early October to mid-November, has the clearest skies and the most reliable views, with cold nights that drop well below freezing at Lamuney. It is also the busiest time, so campsites fill and permits and agencies need booking weeks ahead.

Some agencies run treks to Dzongri in December and early spring, when there is snow on the trail and nights are bitterly cold. The monsoon, from June to September, is not trekking season: the trail is muddy and full of leeches, views are nil and the park may be closed. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: What it costs
paras: Most people trek through an agency on a fixed package that includes permits for the guide and crew, tents or lodges, all meals on the trail, a cook, porters or pack animals, and the guide. Indicative 2025–26 prices for the full Goecha La trek run from about ₹14,000–18,000 per person with large group operators to ₹22,000–30,000 or more with smaller, better-equipped local agencies. Dzongri-only treks cost about ₹10,000–20,000.

On top of the package, budget for park fees for yourself if not included, transport to Yuksom (shared jeep from Siliguri about ₹450–550, or a reserved car about ₹6,500–8,000), a night or two in Yuksom before and after, a personal porter if you want one (about ₹1,000–1,500 a day), and tips for the crew. Foreign nationals pay higher park fees and usually higher package rates.
list: Ask exactly what is included: park fees, sleeping bags, tents, meals, pack animals, transport.
Ask how many trekkers per guide, and whether the guide is registered and trained in first aid.
Ask what happens if you must turn back: who walks down with you, and what is refunded.

sections.heading: Altitude and safety
paras: The trek gains height fast. From Yuksom at 1,780 m you sleep at about 3,000 m on the first night and about 4,000 m on the second. That is quicker than most medical guidance suggests, which is why the rest day at Dzongri matters so much. Headaches, poor sleep and loss of appetite are common on the first nights. Worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, unsteady walking or breathlessness at rest are signs of serious altitude illness: the cure is to go down at once.

Walk slowly from the first hour, drink water steadily, eat even when you are not hungry, and avoid alcohol. Talk to a doctor before the trek about whether to carry acetazolamide and how to use it. Weather can turn fast: snow is possible above Dzongri in any month, and the summit-day start is cold and dark.

Mobile signal is patchy after Yuksom and absent for much of the route. Tell someone at home your plan and expected return date. Take travel insurance that covers trekking at these heights and emergency evacuation, and read the small print on the altitude limit.

sections.heading: What to pack
paras: Agencies supply tents, kitchen gear and usually sleeping mats; many rent sleeping bags, but bring your own if you can, rated to minus 10°C or lower for October and November. Pack light: porters and pack animals carry the group kit, and a personal porter costs extra.
Leave valuables in Yuksom, but carry your ID and permits in a waterproof pouch on your person. Plastic bottles and wrappers are restricted in the park, and you should carry out all your rubbish.
list: Broken-in trekking boots with ankle support, plus camp shoes
Down jacket, fleece, thermal base layers, waterproof jacket and trousers
Warm hat, sun hat, gloves and spare socks
Sunglasses with good UV protection, sunscreen and lip balm
Refillable water bottles and purification tablets
Personal first-aid kit and any prescribed medicines
Trekking poles for the long descents
Leech socks if trekking in late April or May

faqs.q: How many days does the Goecha La trek take
faqs.a: Most itineraries take 8 days of walking from Yuksom and back, and many agencies sell it as 10–11 days door to door from Siliguri or NJP, including the drives and nights in Yuksom. Adding a second rest day makes it safer and more enjoyable. The shorter Dzongri trek takes 4–5 days.

The Goecha La pass is about 4,940 m. In recent seasons trekkers have generally been allowed only as far as View Point 1, at roughly 4,600 m, above Samiti Lake. The highest campsite is Lamuney at about 4,150 m. Rules on how far trekkers can go change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I do the Goecha La trek without an agency
faqs.a: No. Independent trekking is not allowed in Khangchendzonga National Park. You must go with a registered guide, and in practice that means booking through a licensed agency that handles permits, porters, tents and food. Foreign nationals must use a registered Sikkim agency and usually trek in a group of two or more.

faqs.q: What is the best month for Goecha La
faqs.a: October and early November give the clearest views and stable weather, though nights at Lamuney fall well below freezing and campsites are busy. April and May bring rhododendrons and milder nights but more cloud. The trek is not run in the monsoon from June to September. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How fit do I need to be for Goecha La
faqs.a: You should be able to walk 6–8 hours a day for several days in a row, with steep climbs and descents, while carrying a daypack. Start training two months before: long hill walks, stair climbs and cardio three or four times a week. Fitness helps, but anyone can be hit by altitude sickness, so ascend slowly.

faqs.q: What does the Goecha La trek cost
faqs.a: Indicative 2025–26 prices for an agency package run from about ₹14,000–18,000 per person with large group operators to ₹22,000–30,000 or more with smaller local agencies, usually including guide, food, tents and porters. Add park fees if not included, transport to Yuksom, nights in Yuksom and tips. Foreign nationals pay more.

faqs.q: Is there mobile signal on the trek
faqs.a: Signal is good in Yuksom and patchy for the first hours on the trail. It may appear briefly at Tshoka or Dzongri on some networks, but for most of the trek there is none. Agencies may carry a satellite phone or radio for emergencies; ask before you book. Tell family your plan and return date.

faqs.q: Where do trekkers sleep on the route
faqs.a: Most groups sleep in tents pitched by their agency at designated campsites. Basic government trekkers' huts exist at Tshoka, Dzongri and Thansing, with bunk rooms and no heating, used by some groups. Expect cold, simple conditions and shared toilets. Bring a warm sleeping bag even if your agency supplies one.

faqs.q: Can beginners do the Dzongri trek instead
faqs.a: Fit beginners can, with a good agency and a rest day at Dzongri. It is shorter, at 4–5 days, but still climbs to about 4,000 m in two days, so altitude is a real risk. If you have never trekked before, consider a gentler walk first, such as Maenam Hill near Ravangla or Tendong Hill near Namchi.
